summary: Prescription sleep medication for insomnia (trouble falling asleep and/or staying asleep). Works by turning down the brain’s “wake drive,” but can cause next-day sleepiness, vivid dreams, and rare sleep-walking/sleep-driving behaviors.
description: Belsomra is a nightly, as-needed insomnia medication you take within 30 minutes of bedtime (only when you can stay in bed for at least 7 hours). It can help with sleep onset and sleep maintenance. Common side effects include drowsiness, headache, dizziness, and abnormal dreams. It can worsen depression in some people and may trigger rare REM-related effects like sleep paralysis or hallucinations. Avoid alcohol and other sedatives. If insomnia doesn’t improve after 7–10 days, it’s a sign you may need a deeper medical/psychiatric reassessment—not just a stronger sleep med.
patient_summary: Belsomra helps with falling asleep and staying asleep by blocking orexin (a wakefulness signal). Take it within 30 minutes of bedtime only when you can sleep at least 7 hours. Expect possible next-day grogginess and vivid dreams. Rarely, people can do things in their sleep (sleep-walking, sleep-driving) and not remember it—stop the medication and call your prescriber if that happens. Avoid alcohol and other sedatives.

primary.context: FDA-approved for insomnia characterized by difficulty falling asleep and/or staying asleep. Best outcomes usually come from pairing medication with behavioral insomnia treatment (like CBT-I) and sleep schedule work.

secondary.context: Use caution if you have depression—some people experience worsening mood or suicidal thoughts on hypnotics. Lowest effective dose and close follow-up matter.
Use caution in sleep-disordered breathing or significant respiratory disease. If you snore loudly, stop breathing during sleep, or feel unusually sleepy in the day, get evaluated.

therapeutic_response.display: ~30 minutes (can feel slower if taken with or right after food)

common_adverse_effects.incidence: 2% to 7% (reported in labeling; more common in females)
common_adverse_effects.notes: This is the big one. If you don’t get a full night in bed, or you take it with food, you’re more likely to feel groggy the next day. If you drive for work or operate machinery, be extra cautious.

common_adverse_effects.incidence: 7% (reported in labeling; more common in females)
common_adverse_effects.notes: Usually mild, sometimes dose-related. If headaches become persistent or severe, it’s worth reassessing dose and sleep schedule.
Can show up at night (bathroom trips) or in the morning. Get up slowly and be careful with falls—especially if you’re older or taking other sedating meds.
Dreams can feel vivid, intense, or strange. If it’s tolerable, it’s usually just annoying. If it’s distressing or triggers worsening mood, that’s a reason to stop or switch.
Hydration, sugar-free gum, or mouth rinse can help. If dry mouth becomes severe, talk with your prescriber.
Usually mild. If persistent, consider timing, diet, and other meds that may be contributing.

serious_risks.risk: Complex sleep behaviors: sleep-walking, sleep-driving, preparing food, making calls, or having sex while not fully awake—often with no memory afterward. Stop immediately and contact your prescriber.
Mood worsening: exacerbation of depression, suicidal ideation—especially in people with depression or significant mood instability. Use the smallest effective dose and keep close follow-up.
REM-related events: sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, and cataplexy-like lower extremity weakness (leg weakness can happen at night or during the day).
CNS depression and next-day impairment: slowed reaction time, poor judgment, increased accident risk—especially if you combine with other sedatives or don’t get enough sleep time.
Respiratory risk in vulnerable people: caution if you have respiratory compromise (severe COPD or severe OSA).

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to suvorexant or any component of the formulation (noted in some non-US labeling)

precautions: Contraindicated in narcolepsy (it targets the orexin system tied to wakefulness)
CNS depression: can impair driving, reaction time, and decision-making the next day
Complex sleep behaviors (sleep-walking, sleep-driving, eating, calling people, sex) can occur and you may not remember it—stop immediately if this happens
REM-related effects may occur: sleep paralysis, hallucinations around sleep-wake transitions, and cataplexy-like leg weakness
Depression risk: hypnotics can worsen depression or suicidal thinking in some people—use caution and keep doses minimal
Respiratory caution: use carefully in people with significant breathing issues (severe COPD or severe obstructive sleep apnea hasn’t been well studied)

interactions.mechanism: Additive CNS depression: worsened sedation, impaired coordination/judgment, and higher risk of dangerous sleep behaviors.
interactions.action: Avoid. If you drink, skip Belsomra that night.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, other sleep meds)
interactions.mechanism: More sedation, more next-day impairment, higher fall risk, and higher risk of complex sleep behaviors.
interactions.action: Avoid stacking sedatives unless your prescriber explicitly instructs it. If combined, use the lowest effective doses and monitor next-day functioning.

interactions.interactant: Strong or moderate CYP3A inhibitors (some antifungals, certain antibiotics, some HIV/HCV meds, etc.)
interactions.mechanism: Higher suvorexant exposure → more sedation, more next-day impairment, more adverse effects.
interactions.action: Dose adjustments or avoidance may be needed. If you’re starting a new medication, ask specifically about CYP3A interactions.

interactions.interactant: CYP3A inducers (some seizure meds, rifampin, St. John’s wort)
interactions.mechanism: Lower suvorexant levels → reduced sleep benefit.
interactions.action: May make Belsomra feel like it “stopped working.” Consider alternatives rather than escalating without a plan.

interactions.mechanism: Can increase suvorexant levels and side effects.
interactions.action: Avoid grapefruit products, or use extra caution and consider lower dosing if grapefruit exposure is unavoidable.

interactions.interactant: Food (especially a meal right before dosing)
interactions.mechanism: Delayed onset and delayed peak effect, which can make it feel inconsistent.
interactions.action: For faster sleep onset, don’t take with or immediately after a meal.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Daytime alertness and next-day impairment: morning grogginess, slowed reaction time, driving safety, workplace function
Sleep behaviors and safety: sleep-walking, sleep-driving, eating, phone calls, sex while not fully awake (stop immediately if any occur)
Mood and suicidality: worsening depression, irritability, suicidal thoughts—especially in patients with depression or mood instability
REM-related effects: sleep paralysis, hallucinations around sleep-wake transitions, cataplexy-like leg weakness
Respiratory status in at-risk patients: worsening snoring, breathing pauses, daytime sleepiness; caution in significant COPD/OSA
Tolerance, misuse, and dependence risk: especially with prolonged use, history of substance use disorder, or combining with alcohol/other sedatives
Response pattern: sleep onset vs sleep maintenance improvement, total sleep time, awakenings, and whether insomnia is resolving or just being masked

special_populations.pregnancy: Animal studies have shown adverse events at certain exposures. In humans, pregnancy data are limited. If insomnia is related to anxiety, depression, trauma, or pregnancy discomfort, nonmedication approaches (CBT-I, schedule support, treating mood/anxiety) are often preferred. Use the lowest effective dose only if benefits clearly outweigh risks and alternatives are not workable.
special_populations.lactation: Suvorexant and a metabolite are present in human milk. Available data suggest low infant exposure (reported relative infant dose <1% in labeling; one small study estimated very low exposure as well). Even with low exposure, monitor the infant for excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, or unusual behavior. The decision to breastfeed while taking Belsomra should weigh infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and the benefit of treatment to the mother.
special_populations.pediatric: Very limited data. Off-label use has been reported in children ≥10 years and adolescents, typically 10–20 mg at bedtime (maximum 20 mg/day), with a strong preference for the lowest effective dose. Some patients discontinue due to abnormal dreams or excessive sleepiness. Use should be cautious, individualized, and typically reserved for specialist situations where behavioral approaches and underlying psychiatric drivers are being actively treated.
special_populations.geriatric: Refer to adult dosing. Older adults can be more sensitive to next-day impairment and falls. Use the lowest effective dose and reassess frequently for daytime sedation, balance issues, and cognitive slowing.
special_populations.renal_impairment: No dosage adjustment necessary based on adult data.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Mild to moderate impairment: no adjustment typically needed, but monitor for increased sedation. Severe impairment: use is not recommended (not studied).

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Bioavailability ~82%; absorption can be delayed with food and decreases at higher doses
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: ~2 hours (range: 30 minutes to 6 hours); delayed ~1.5 hours with a meal
pharmacokinetics.half_life: ~12 hours (terminal half-life ~15 hours; can be longer with moderate hepatic impairment)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via CYP3A4 (major) with minor CYP2C19; hydroxy-suvorexant metabolite is inactive
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Meal delays time to peak and can delay onset; for faster sleep onset, avoid taking with or immediately after food

dosing.titration: Belsomra is taken once nightly, as needed, right before bed—only when you can stay in bed for at least 7 hours. Start low and only increase if you truly need it and you’re not getting next-day impairment.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Belsomra is not a benzodiazepine and it’s not typically associated with dangerous withdrawal the way benzos can be. Most people can stop it without a formal taper. That said, if you’ve been taking it nightly for a long time, you may notice rebound insomnia (sleep feels worse for a bit) just because your brain got used to having a sleep aid onboard.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Belsomra is used for insomnia when your brain won’t “power down”—either you can’t fall asleep, you can’t stay asleep, or both. It’s a symptomatic sleep medication, not a cure for the underlying drivers of insomnia, so it works best when paired with behavioral sleep treatment (like CBT-I) and a real look at what’s keeping sleep stuck.
items: {link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia}: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early
Sleep onset insomnia: You’re in bed, tired, and still awake
Sleep maintenance insomnia: You fall asleep but wake up and can’t get back down

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It didn’t smash me into sleep—it just made it easier to drift off.
I still woke up sometimes, but getting back to sleep felt more doable.
My brain felt less ‘on’ at night.

items.category: Next-day grogginess (especially if you don’t get a full night)
quotes: If I didn’t get at least 7 hours, I felt foggy the next day.
A little hangover-ish the next morning.

items.note: This risk goes up with higher doses, taking it with food, or mixing it with other sedating meds.

quotes: I did something at night and didn’t remember it at all.
My partner said I was up and moving, but I was basically asleep.
That scared me—I stopped it right away.
items.note: If you ever sleep-walk, sleep-drive, or do activities while not fully awake, stop the medication and contact your prescriber immediately.

sections.intro: People describe Belsomra as “turning down wakefulness” more than “knocking you out.” Here are the common themes:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Belsomra is meant to be taken right before bed, but timing matters. It works best when you take it on an empty-ish stomach and only when you can commit to a full night in bed.
key_points: ~30 minutes: Onset can begin (may feel slower if taken with a meal)
~2 hours: Peak levels for many people (wide range)
≥7 hours: Minimum time you should have available for sleep before driving or being active
~12 hours: Average elimination half-life (next-day effects are possible)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Belsomra can help you fall asleep and/or stay asleep, especially when nighttime wakefulness feels like the main problem. But it’s not magic—and if your insomnia is being driven by anxiety loops, depression, trauma nightmares, late-night screens, irregular schedules, substances, or untreated sleep apnea, you’ll get a lot more traction by treating the root cause too.
sections.metric: Sleep onset and sleep maintenance benefit
sections.clinical_details: Longer-term experience suggests some people maintain benefit over extended use, but insomnia meds are usually best as a targeted tool—ideally paired with CBT-I and a plan to avoid drifting into indefinite nightly use unless the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Only take Belsomra when you can stay in bed a full night (at least 7 hours). Next-day impairment is real—especially at higher doses or if you take it with food.

Depression risk: hypnotics can worsen depression or suicidal thinking in some people—use caution and keep doses minimal

patient_counseling: Take within 30 minutes of bedtime and only if you can sleep at least 7 hours before you need to be up and active.
Don’t drive the next morning if you feel sleepy, slowed down, or not fully sharp.
Avoid alcohol and avoid stacking it with other sedating meds unless your prescriber explicitly okays it.
Stop the medication and contact your prescriber immediately if you sleep-walk, sleep-drive, or do activities while not fully awake.
If insomnia doesn’t improve after 7–10 days, don’t just keep escalating—get reassessed for underlying causes (anxiety, depression, substance effects, sleep apnea, circadian rhythm issues).
If you have depression, past suicidal thoughts, or a history of substance misuse, tell your prescriber before starting.

sections.intro: Belsomra is mainly metabolized by CYP3A4. Medications or foods that change CYP3A activity can push levels up (more side effects) or down (less benefit).

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Belsomra is not a benzodiazepine and it’s not typically associated with dangerous withdrawal the way benzos can be. Most people can stop it without a formal taper. That said, if you’ve been taking it nightly for a long time, you may notice rebound insomnia (sleep feels worse for a bit) just because your brain got used to having a sleep aid onboard.
key_points: Most patients can stop without tapering, especially if use was intermittent/as-needed.
If you’ve been taking it nightly long-term and you’re anxious about stopping, a step-down approach can be reasonable (lower dose or fewer nights per week) to reduce rebound insomnia stress.

If sleep worsens after stopping, treat the underlying insomnia drivers (CBT-I, schedule consistency, stimulus control, anxiety/depression treatment) rather than immediately restarting indefinite nightly medication.
If mood worsens or suicidal thoughts appear during discontinuation (or during use), contact your prescriber urgently.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Belsomra is taken once nightly, as needed, right before bed—only when you can stay in bed for at least 7 hours. Start low and only increase if you truly need it and you’re not getting next-day impairment.

adult.prn_use: 10 mg PO once nightly as needed within 30 minutes of bedtime and only when ≥7 hours remain before planned awakening. If needed and tolerated, may increase to 20 mg once nightly. Maximum: 20 mg per night.

sections.simple_explanation: This is a “turn down wakefulness” sleep medicine. It’s not meant for middle-of-the-night redosing, and it’s not a good fit if you can’t reliably sleep at least 7 hours. Taking it with food can delay onset, which can make it feel less predictable.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Special populations matter with Belsomra because exposure (drug levels) can be higher in women and in obesity, and the medication can cause next-day impairment. Severe liver impairment is a no-go.
sections.pregnancy: Animal studies have shown adverse events at certain exposures. In humans, pregnancy data are limited. If insomnia is related to anxiety, depression, trauma, or pregnancy discomfort, nonmedication approaches (CBT-I, schedule support, treating mood/anxiety) are often preferred. Use the lowest effective dose only if benefits clearly outweigh risks and alternatives are not workable.
sections.lactation: Suvorexant and a metabolite are present in human milk. Available data suggest low infant exposure (reported relative infant dose <1% in labeling; one small study estimated very low exposure as well). Even with low exposure, monitor the infant for excessive sleepiness, poor feeding, or unusual behavior. The decision to breastfeed while taking Belsomra should weigh infant exposure risk, breastfeeding benefits, and the benefit of treatment to the mother.
sections.pediatrics: Very limited data. Off-label use has been reported in children ≥10 years and adolescents, typically 10–20 mg at bedtime (maximum 20 mg/day), with a strong preference for the lowest effective dose. Some patients discontinue due to abnormal dreams or excessive sleepiness. Use should be cautious, individualized, and typically reserved for specialist situations where behavioral approaches and underlying psychiatric drivers are being actively treated.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing. Older adults can be more sensitive to next-day impairment and falls. Use the lowest effective dose and reassess frequently for daytime sedation, balance issues, and cognitive slowing.
sections.hepatic: Mild to moderate impairment: no adjustment typically needed, but monitor for increased sedation. Severe impairment: use is not recommended (not studied).
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment necessary based on adult data.
sections.obesity: Exposure is increased in obesity, especially in obese women. Consider the higher risk of exposure-related adverse effects (next-day impairment, sedation, abnormal dreams) before increasing the dose.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Belsomra is an oral tablet. Different strengths make it easier to start low and only increase if needed.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Belsomra blocks orexin receptors (OX1R and OX2R). Orexin is one of the brain’s main “stay awake” signals. When you block that wake drive, sleep is easier to initiate and maintain. Because orexin is tied to narcolepsy biology, blocking it can also explain rare narcolepsy-like side effects (sleep paralysis, hallucinations, cataplexy-like weakness).

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Belsomra can be a reasonable option when insomnia is persistent and you’ve already addressed the basics (sleep schedule, screens, caffeine, alcohol, nighttime worry loops) and/or tried evidence-based behavioral treatment like CBT-I. It’s not a substitute for treating anxiety, depression, PTSD nightmares, circadian rhythm disruption, or sleep apnea—because those will keep re-breaking sleep no matter what pill you use. If you need an insomnia med beyond a few weeks, it usually means the underlying cause still needs attention.

faqs.a: Belsomra (suvorexant) is used to treat insomnia—meaning difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It’s designed for nights when sleep won’t happen naturally, and it works best when paired with behavioral sleep treatment (like CBT-I) and a plan to address what’s driving the insomnia.

faqs.q: How do I take Belsomra correctly?
faqs.a: Take it within 30 minutes of bedtime, only if you can stay in bed for at least 7 hours before you need to be up and active. It can be taken with or without food, but if you take it with a meal (or right after eating), it may kick in later and feel less predictable.

faqs.q: What dose should I start with?
faqs.a: Most adults start at 10 mg once nightly as needed. If it’s not enough and you tolerate it without next-day impairment, it may be increased up to 20 mg nightly. The maximum is 20 mg per night.

Many people feel it starting within about 30 minutes, but it can vary. Food can delay onset, and peak levels often occur around 2 hours (with a wide range). That’s why it’s meant to be taken right before bed—not earlier in the evening.

faqs.q: Can I drive the next morning?
faqs.a: Maybe—but only if you feel fully alert. Belsomra can cause next-day impairment, especially if you don’t get a full 7 hours in bed, if you take a higher dose, or if you combine it with other sedatives. If you feel sleepy, foggy, or slowed down, don’t drive.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: The most common ones are drowsiness/daytime sleepiness, headache, dizziness, abnormal/vivid dreams, dry mouth, and diarrhea. Side effects are more likely at higher doses and when combined with other sedating substances.

faqs.q: Can Belsomra cause sleep paralysis or hallucinations?
faqs.a: Yes, it can. Because it affects the orexin system (which helps regulate wakefulness and REM sleep), some people experience REM-related effects like sleep paralysis, hallucinations around sleep-wake transitions, or cataplexy-like leg weakness. If this happens, contact your prescriber—especially if it feels intense or unsafe.

faqs.q: What are “complex sleep behaviors,” and how serious are they?
faqs.a: These are activities like sleep-walking, sleep-driving, cooking/eating, making phone calls, or having sex while not fully awake—often with no memory afterward. They’re rare, but serious. If it happens even once, stop Belsomra immediately and contact your prescriber.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with Belsomra?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol increases sedation, impairment, and the risk of unsafe sleep behaviors. If you drink that night, skip Belsomra.

People with narcolepsy should not take it. It’s also not recommended in severe liver impairment. If you have significant breathing problems (like severe COPD or severe obstructive sleep apnea), depression with suicidal thoughts, or a history of substance misuse, you need a careful risk-benefit conversation before using it.

It’s a Schedule IV medication, and risk of misuse can be higher with prolonged use or in people with substance use history—especially if combined with alcohol or other sedating drugs. It’s not a benzodiazepine, but “scheduled” still means you should use it carefully, at the lowest effective dose, and with a plan.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off Belsomra?
faqs.a: Usually, no. Most people can stop without a formal taper. The main issue can be rebound insomnia (sleep feels worse temporarily) if you’ve been taking it nightly for a long time. If you’re worried, stepping down dose or using it fewer nights per week can make the transition easier.

faqs.q: What if my insomnia doesn’t improve after a week?
faqs.a: If sleep doesn’t improve after 7–10 days, that’s a flag to reassess what’s causing the insomnia. Persistent insomnia often has an underlying driver—anxiety loops, depression, trauma, circadian rhythm problems, substances, medical issues, or sleep apnea—and fixing that driver is what creates durable sleep.
